title: Abstention, coverage and decision costs

key_terms.Coverage: The fraction of requests a selective system answers instead of abstaining or routing to review.
key_terms.Selective risk: The expected loss among answered requests, undefined when nothing is answered.
key_terms.Risk-coverage curve: A plot of selective risk against coverage across thresholds.
key_terms.Abstention threshold: The score cutoff below which the system abstains, ideally chosen on development data rather than reported on it.
key_terms.Calibrated probability: A score whose stated probability of correctness matches observed accuracy, which a confidence-like number need not do.

outcome: Choose and evaluate an abstention policy with explicit costs, coverage and held-out evidence instead of reporting only conditional accuracy.
verification: Answering everything gives coverage 1, accuracy 0.5 and cost 2.5; abstaining on everything gives coverage 0, missing accuracy and cost 0.4; the calibrated-probability cutoff is 0.92; subgroup counts, coverage and cost are reported separately.

exercises.title: Answer everything
exercises.task: Use threshold 0 on the development fixture.
exercises.hint: Two of four answers are wrong.
exercises.answer: The policy pays 5 twice and averages over all four eligible requests.

reasoning.approach: Call `policy_metrics([0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2], [1, 0, 1, 0], 0)`. Every score is at least 0, so every request is answered.
reasoning.why: Coverage is 4 / 4 = 1. Two answers are correct, so accuracy is 0.5. The two wrong answers cost 5 each, and correct answers cost 0, so the mean cost is (0 + 5 + 0 + 5) / 4 = 2.5.
reasoning.pitfall: Choosing the policy with the highest coverage because it helps the most users ignores the cost structure. A wrong answer costs 12.5 times an abstention here, so answering everything is the most expensive option in the fixture.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `policy_metrics([1, 0], [1, 0], 0)["coverage"] == 1`. Run the four-row call above and confirm the cost is 2.5.

exercises.title: Abstain on everything
exercises.task: Choose a threshold above every score.
exercises.expected: Coverage 0, missing conditional accuracy and cost 0.4.
exercises.hint: An empty answered set is not perfect accuracy.
exercises.answer: The operational cost remains defined because every eligible request incurs the abstention cost.

reasoning.approach: Use a threshold above every development score, such as 0.95. No score is at least 0.95, so every request abstains.
reasoning.why: Coverage is 0, and conditional accuracy has no answered rows, so the function returns `None`. Cost is still defined: every request pays the abstention cost 0.4, so the mean is 0.4.
reasoning.pitfall: Dropping abstained requests from the cost would make the always-abstain policy cost 0. The cost is averaged over all eligible requests because declining to answer is a real outcome for the person who asked.
reasoning.verify: Call `policy_metrics([0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2], [1, 0, 1, 0], 0.95)` and confirm `coverage == 0`, `accuracy is None` and `cost` equals 0.4. The single-row check `policy_metrics([0.4], [1], 0.5)["cost"] == 0.4` shows the same rule.

exercises.title: Check equality
exercises.answer: Boundary behavior matters for reproducibility and should be written into the policy contract.

reasoning.approach: Call `policy_metrics([0.5], [1], 0.5)`. The rule is `p >= threshold`, so a score equal to the threshold is answered.
reasoning.why: Coverage is 1 because 0.5 >= 0.5. Scores are often rounded, so many requests can sit exactly at a threshold; the inclusive rule decides all of them the same way every run.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing `>` in one implementation and `>=` in another seems trivial, but with rounded scores the two policies can differ on many requests, and their coverage and cost will not reproduce across systems.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `policy_metrics([0.5], [1], 0.5)["coverage"] == 1`. Write the inclusive rule into the policy description that ships with the threshold.

exercises.title: Derive the probability cutoff
exercises.task: Use wrong-answer cost 5 and abstention cost 0.4.
exercises.answer: The derivation assumes calibrated correctness probabilities and zero cost for correct answers. It does not justify using 0.92 on an arbitrary score.

reasoning.approach: Set expected costs equal. Answering costs `wrong_cost` times the probability of being wrong, 5 times (1 - p); abstaining costs 0.4. Answer when 5 (1 - p) <= 0.4.
reasoning.why: Solving gives 1 - p <= 0.08, so p >= 0.92. Worked case A asserts `np.isclose(1 - 0.4 / 5, 0.92)`. The derivation assumes p is a calibrated probability of correctness and correct answers cost nothing.
reasoning.pitfall: Plugging 0.92 into a raw model score that is not calibrated is the mistake. Case A's development search chose 0.85 on these scores, and case B shows scores of 0.99 and 0.97 that were both wrong, so these scores are not calibrated probabilities.
reasoning.verify: Check that `1 - 0.4 / 5 == 0.92` and then verify calibration separately (eval-011) before using the formula on any score.

exercises.title: Inspect subgroup coverage
exercises.task: Compute the policy separately for routine and rare requests.
exercises.expected: Report each eligible count, coverage and cost.
exercises.hint: Overall utility can hide service allocation.
exercises.answer: Differences can reflect calibration, difficulty or selection. Preserve group definitions and uncertainty before attributing them to a model mechanism.

reasoning.approach: Split the eligible requests by group, run `policy_metrics` once per group with the same frozen threshold, and report eligible count, coverage, conditional accuracy and cost for each.
reasoning.why: The overall coverage is a weighted mix of group coverages. If rare requests get lower scores, they abstain more often, and the overall number hides that rare users receive answers far less often than routine users.
reasoning.pitfall: Concluding that the model is biased against rare requests from a coverage gap alone skips other explanations: rare requests may be harder, the scores may be miscalibrated for them, or the groups may have been sampled differently.
reasoning.verify: Check that the group eligible counts sum to the total and that the count-weighted group costs reproduce the overall cost. Report intervals because rare groups will usually be small.

exercises.title: Protect the final set
exercises.task: The held-out case exposes a bad threshold. What follows?
exercises.expected: Use it as a diagnosis and collect a new final assessment after changes.
exercises.hint: Changing the policy consumes the old holdout.
exercises.answer: A test failure can guide development, but the same labels cannot remain untouched evidence for the modified policy.

reasoning.approach: Treat the held-out failure as diagnostic. Case B applies the frozen 0.85 threshold to new outcomes and gets coverage 0.5, accuracy 0 and cost 2.7, which shows the development threshold does not transfer.
reasoning.why: The two confident answers (scores 0.99 and 0.97) were wrong, costing 5 each, and two abstentions cost 0.4 each, so the mean is (5 + 5 + 0.4 + 0.4) / 4 = 2.7. That is worse than always abstaining at 0.4.
reasoning.pitfall: Retuning the threshold on the same held-out rows and reporting the new held-out cost is the mistake. The rows have now shaped the policy, so their cost is a development number and overstates performance.
reasoning.verify: Worked case B asserts `coverage == 0.5`, `accuracy == 0` and `np.isclose(cost, 2.7)`. After any change, collect a fresh final set and freeze the policy before scoring it.
